6.70.oldText: “Wah!” said Little Toomai, and his eyes were very heavy. “Kala Nag, my lord, let us keep by Pudmini and go to Petersen Sahib’s camp, or I shall drop from your neck.”

6.71.oldText: The third elephant watched the two go away, snorted, wheeled round, and took his own path. He may have belonged to some little local king’s establishment, fifty or sixty or a hundred miles away.

6.72.oldText: Two hours later, as Petersen Sahib was eating early breakfast, his elephants—who had been double chained that night—began to trumpet, and Pudmini, mired to the shoulders, with Kala Nag, very footsore, shambled into the camp. Little Toomai’s face was gray and pinched, and his hair was full of leaves and drenched with dew, but he tried to salute Petersen Sahib, and cried faintly: “The dance—the elephant dance! I have seen it, and—I die!” As Kala Nag sat down, he slid off his neck in a dead faint.

6.73.oldText: But, since the village children have nerves of iron, in two hours he was lying very contentedly in Petersen Sahib’s hammock, with Petersen Sahib’s shooting-coat under his head and a glass of warm milk, a little brandy, with a dash of quinine, inside him. The old hairy, scarred hunters of the jungles sat three deep before him, looking at him as though he were a spirit, while he told his tale in short words, as a child will, and wound up with:

6.74.oldText: “Now, if I lie in one word, send men to see, and they will find that the elephant folk have trampled down more room in their dance-room, and they will find ten and ten, and many times ten, tracks leading to that dance-room. They made more room with their feet. I have seen it. Kala Nag took me, and I saw. Also Kala Nag is very leg-weary!”

6.75.oldText: Little Toomai lay back and slept all through the long afternoon and into the twilight. While he slept Petersen Sahib and Machua Appa followed the track of the two elephants for fifteen miles across the hills. Petersen Sahib had spent eighteen years catching elephants, and he had only once before found such a dance-place. Machua Appa had no need to look twice at the clearing to see what had been done there, or to scratch with his toe in the packed, rammed earth.

6.76.oldText: “The child speaks truth,” said he. “All this was done last night, and I have counted seventy tracks crossing the river. See, Sahib, where Pudmini’s leg-iron cut the bark of that tree! Yes; she was there too.”

6.77.oldText: They looked at one another and up and down, and they wondered. For the ways of elephants are beyond the wit of any man to fathom.

6.78.oldText: “Forty years and five,” said Machua Appa, “have I followed my lord, the elephant, but never have I heard that any child of man had seen what this child has seen. By all the Gods of the Hills, it is—what can we say?” And he shook his head.

6.79.oldText: When they got back to camp it was time for the evening meal. Petersen Sahib ate alone in his tent, but he gave orders that the camp should have two sheep and some fowls, as well as a double ration of flour and rice and salt, for he knew there would be a feast.

6.80.oldText: Big Toomai had come up hotfoot from the camp in the plains to search for his son and his elephant. Now that he had found them he looked at them as though he were afraid of them both. And there was a feast by the blazing campfires in front of the lines of picketed elephants, and Little Toomai was the hero of it all. The big brown elephant catchers, the trackers and drivers and ropers, and the men who knew all the secrets of breaking the wildest elephants, passed him from one to the other. They marked his forehead with blood from the breast of a newly killed jungle-cock to show that he was a forester, initiated and free of all the jungles.

6.81.oldText: At last, when the flames died down and the red light of the logs made the elephants look as though they had been dipped in blood too, Machua Appa, the head of all the drivers of all the Keddahs—Machua Appa, Petersen Sahib’s other self, who had never seen a made road in forty years; Machua Appa, who was so great that he had no other name than Machua Appa—leaped to his feet, with Little Toomai held high in the air above his head, and shouted: “Listen, my brothers. Listen, too, you my lords in the lines there, for I, Machua Appa, am speaking! This little one shall no more be called Little Toomai, but Toomai of the Elephants, as his great-grandfather was called before him. What no man has seen he has seen through the long night, and the favor of the elephant-folk and of the Gods of the Jungles is with him. He shall become a great tracker. He shall become greater than I, even I, Machua Appa! He shall follow the new trail, and the stale trail, and the mixed trail, with a clear eye! He shall take no harm in the Keddah when he runs under their bellies to rope the wild tuskers; and if he slips before the feet of the charging bull elephant, the bull elephant shall know who he is and shall not crush him. Aihai! my lords in the chains,”—he whirled up the line of pickets—“here is the little one that has seen your dances in your hidden places—the sight that no man has ever seen! Give him honor, my lords! Salaam karo, my children. Make your salute to Toomai of the Elephants! Gunga Pershad, ahaa! Hira Guj, Birchi Guj, Kuttar Guj, ahaa! Pudmini—you have seen him at the dance, and you too, Kala Nag, my pearl among elephants!—ahaa! Together! To Toomai of the Elephants. Barrao!”

6.82.oldText: And at that last wild yell the whole line flung up their trunks till the tips touched their foreheads, and broke out into the full salute—the crashing trumpet-peal that only the Viceroy of India hears, the Salaamut of the Keddah.

6.83.oldText: But it was all for the sake of Little Toomai, who had seen what no one had seen before—the dance of the elephants at night and alone in the heart of the Garo hills!

6.85.oldText: (The song that Toomai’s mother sang to the baby)

6.86.oldText:
Shiv, who poured the harvest and made the winds to blow,
Sitting at the doorways of a day of long ago,
Gave to each his portion, food and toil and fate,
From the King upon the _guddee_ to the Beggar at the gate.
_All things made he—Shiva the Preserver.
Mahadeo!  Mahadeo!  He made all,—
Thorn for the camel, fodder for the kine,
And mother’s heart for sleepy head, O little son of mine!_

6.87.oldText:
Wheat he gave to rich folk, millet to the poor,
Broken scraps for holy men that beg from door to door;
Battle to the tiger, carrion to the kite,
And rags and bones to wicked wolves without the wall at night.
Naught he found too lofty, none he saw too low—
Parbati beside him watched them come and go;
Thought to cheat her husband, turning Shiv to jest—
Stole the little grasshopper and hid it in her breast.
_So she tricked him, Shiva the Preserver.
Mahadeo!  Mahadeo!  Turn and see.
Tall are the camels, heavy are the kine,
But this was Least of Little Things, O little son of mine!_

6.88.oldText:
When the dole was ended, laughingly she said,
“Master, of a million mouths, is not one unfed?”
Laughing, Shiv made answer, “All have had their part,
Even he, the little one, hidden ’neath your heart.”
From her breast she plucked it, Parbati the thief,
Saw the Least of Little Things gnawed a new-grown leaf!
Saw and feared and wondered, making prayer to Shiv,
Who hath surely given meat to all that live.
_All things made he—Shiva the Preserver.
Mahadeo!  Mahadeo!  He made all,—
Thorn for the camel, fodder for the kine,
And mother’s heart for sleepy head, O little son of mine!_

7.0.oldText:
You can work it out by Fractions or by simple Rule of Three,
But the way of Tweedle-dum is not the way of Tweedle-dee.
You can twist it, you can turn it, you can plait it till you drop,
But the way of Pilly Winky’s not the way of Winkie Pop!

7.1.oldText: It had been raining heavily for one whole month—raining on a camp of thirty thousand men and thousands of camels, elephants, horses, bullocks, and mules all gathered together at a place called Rawal Pindi, to be reviewed by the Viceroy of India. He was receiving a visit from the Amir of Afghanistan—a wild king of a very wild country. The Amir had brought with him as a bodyguard eight hundred men and horses who had never seen a camp or a locomotive before in their lives—savage men and savage horses from somewhere at the back of Central Asia. Every night a mob of these horses would be sure to break their heel ropes and stampede up and down the camp through the mud in the dark, or the camels would break loose and run about and trip over the ropes of the tents. You can imagine how pleasant that was for men trying to sleep. My tent was far from the camel lines, and I thought it was safe. But one night a man popped his head in and shouted, “Get out, quick! They’re coming! My tent’s gone!”

7.2.oldText: I knew who “they” were, so I put on my boots and waterproof and scuttled out into the slush. Little Vixen, my fox terrier, went out through the other side. Then there was a roaring and a grunting and bubbling, and I saw the tent cave in as the pole snapped and start to dance about like a mad ghost. A camel had blundered into it, and wet and angry as I was, I could not help laughing. Then I ran on, because I did not know how many camels might have got loose, and before long I was out of sight of the camp, plowing my way through the mud.

7.3.oldText: At last I fell over the tail end of a gun, and from that I knew I was somewhere near the artillery lines where the cannon were stacked at night. As I did not want to splash about any more in the drizzle and the dark, I put my waterproof over the muzzle of one gun, made a sort of wigwam with two or three rammers I found, and lay along the tail of another gun, wondering where Vixen had got to and where I might be.

7.4.oldText: Just as I was getting ready to sleep I heard a jingle of harness and a grunt, and a mule passed me shaking his wet ears. He belonged to a screw-gun battery, because I could hear the rattle of the straps and rings and chains and things on his saddle pad. The screw-guns are tiny little cannon made in two pieces, that are screwed together when the time comes to use them. They are taken up mountains, anywhere a mule can find a road, and they are very useful for fighting in rocky country.

7.5.oldText: Behind the mule there was a camel, his big soft feet squelching and slipping in the mud, and his neck bobbing to and fro like a strayed hen’s. Luckily, I knew enough beast language from the natives—not wild-beast language, but camp-beast language, of course—to know what he was saying.

7.6.oldText: He must have been the one that flopped into my tent, because he called to the mule, “What shall I do? Where shall I go? I have fought with a white thing that waved, and it took a stick and hit me on the neck.” (That was my broken tent pole, and I was very glad to know it.) “Shall we run on?”

7.7.oldText: “Oh, it was you,” said the mule, “you and your friends, who have been disturbing the camp? All right. You’ll be beaten for this in the morning. But I may as well give you something on account now.”

7.8.oldText: I heard the harness jingle as the mule backed up and caught the camel two kicks in the ribs that rang like a drum. “Another time,” he said, “you’ll know better than to run through a mule battery at night, shouting ‘Thieves and fire!’ Sit down, and keep your silly neck quiet.”

7.9.oldText: The camel doubled up camel-fashion, like a two-foot rule, and sat down whimpering. There was a regular beat of hoofs in the darkness, and a big troop-horse cantered up as steadily as though he were on parade, jumped a gun tail, and landed close to the mule.

7.10.oldText: “It’s disgraceful,” he said, blowing out his nostrils. “Those camels have racketed through our lines again—the third time this week. How’s a horse to keep his condition if he isn’t allowed to sleep? Who’s here?”

7.11.oldText: “I’m the breech-piece mule of number two gun of the First Screw Battery,” said the mule, “and the other’s one of your friends. He’s woken me up too. Who are you?”

7.12.oldText: “Number Fifteen, E troop, Ninth Lancers—Dick Cunliffe’s horse. Stand over a little, there.”

7.13.oldText: “Oh, beg your pardon,” said the mule. “It’s too dark to see much. Aren’t these camels too sickening for anything? I walked out of my lines to get a little peace and quiet here.”

7.14.oldText: “My lords,” said the camel humbly, “we dreamed bad dreams in the night, and we were very much afraid. I am only a baggage camel of the 39th Native Infantry, and I am not as brave as you are, my lords.”

7.15.oldText: “Then why didn’t you stay and carry baggage for the 39th Native Infantry, instead of running all over the camp?” said the mule.

7.16.oldText: “They were such very bad dreams,” said the camel. “I am sorry. Listen! What is that? Shall we run on again?”

7.17.oldText: “Sit down,” said the mule, “or you’ll snap your long stick-legs between the guns.” He cocked one ear and listened. “Bullocks!” he said. “Gun bullocks. Honestly, you and your friends have woken the camp very thoroughly. It takes a good deal of prodding to get a gun-bullock up.”

7.18.oldText: I heard a chain dragging along the ground, and a yoke of the great sulky white bullocks that drag the heavy siege guns when the elephants won’t go any nearer to the firing came shouldering along together. Almost stepping on the chain was another battery mule, calling wildly for “Billy.”

7.19.oldText: “That’s one of our recruits,” said the old mule to the troop-horse. “He’s calling for me. Here, youngster, stop squealing. The dark never hurt anybody yet.”

7.20.oldText: The gun-bullocks lay down together and began chewing the cud, but the young mule huddled close to Billy.

7.21.oldText: “Things!” he said. “Fearful and horrible, Billy! They came into our lines while we were asleep. Do you think they’ll kill us?”

7.22.oldText: “I’ve a very great mind to give you a number-one kicking,” said Billy. “The idea of a fourteen-hand mule with your training disgracing the battery in front of this gentleman!”

7.23.oldText: “Gently, gently!” said the troop-horse. “Remember they are always like this to begin with. The first time I ever saw a man (it was in Australia when I was a three-year-old) I ran for half a day, and if I’d seen a camel, I should have been running still.”

7.24.oldText: Nearly all our horses for the English cavalry are brought to India from Australia, and are broken in by the troopers themselves.

7.25.oldText: “True enough,” said Billy. “Stop shaking, youngster. The first time they put the full harness with all its chains on my back I stood on my forelegs and kicked every bit of it off. I hadn’t learned the real science of kicking then, but the battery said they had never seen anything like it.”

7.26.oldText: “But this wasn’t harness or anything that jingled,” said the young mule. “You know I don’t mind that now, Billy. It was Things like trees, and they fell up and down the lines and bubbled. My head-rope broke, and I couldn’t find my driver, and I couldn’t find you, Billy, so I ran off with—with these gentlemen.”

7.27.oldText: “Hm!” said Billy. “As soon as I heard the camels were loose I came away on my own. When a battery—a screw-gun mule calls gun-bullocks gentlemen, he must be very badly shaken up. Who are you fellows on the ground there?”

7.28.oldText: The gun-bullocks rolled their cuds and answered both together: “The seventh yoke of the first gun of the Big Gun Battery. We were asleep when the camels came, but when we were trampled on we got up and walked away. It is better to lie quiet in the mud than to be disturbed on good bedding. We told your friend here that there was nothing to be afraid of, but he knew so much that he thought otherwise. Wah!”

7.30.oldText: “That comes of being afraid,” said Billy. “You get laughed at by gun-bullocks. I hope you like it, young un.”

7.31.oldText: The young mule’s teeth snapped, and I heard him say something about not being afraid of any beefy old bullock in the world. But the bullocks only clicked their horns together and went on chewing.

7.32.oldText: “Now, don’t be angry after you’ve been afraid. That’s the worst kind of cowardice,” said the troop-horse. “Anybody can be forgiven for being scared in the night, I think, if they see things they don’t understand. We’ve broken out of our pickets again and again, four hundred and fifty of us, just because a new recruit got to telling tales of whip snakes at home in Australia, till we were scared to death of the loose ends of our head-ropes.”

7.33.oldText: “That’s all very well in camp,” said Billy. “I’m not above stampeding myself, for the fun of it, when I haven’t been out for a day or two. But what do you do on active service?”

7.34.oldText: “Oh, that’s quite another set of new shoes,” said the troop-horse. “Dick Cunliffe’s on my back then, and drives his knees into me, and all I have to do is watch where I’m putting my feet, keep my hind legs well under me, and be bridle-wise.”

7.36.oldText: “By the Blue Gums of the Back Blocks,” snorted the troop-horse, “do you mean to say you aren’t taught to be bridle-wise in your business? How can you do anything, unless you can spin round at once when the rein is pressed on your neck? It means life or death to your man, and of course that’s life and death to you. Get round with your hind legs under you the instant you feel the rein on your neck. If you haven’t room to swing round, rear up a little and come round on your hind legs. That’s being bridle-wise.”

7.37.oldText: “We aren’t taught that way,” said Billy the mule stiffly. “We’re taught to obey the man at our head: step off when he says so, and step in when he says so. I suppose it comes to the same thing. Now, with all this fancy business and rearing, which must be very bad for your hocks, what do you do?”

7.38.oldText: “That depends,” said the troop-horse. “Generally I have to go in among a lot of yelling, hairy men with knives—long shiny knives, worse than the farrier’s knives—and I have to take care that Dick’s boot is just touching the next man’s boot without crushing it. I can see Dick’s lance to the right of my right eye, and I know I’m safe. I shouldn’t care to be the man or horse that stood up to Dick and me when we’re in a hurry.”

7.39.oldText: “Don’t the knives hurt?” said the young mule.

7.40.oldText: “Well, I got one cut across the chest once, but that wasn’t Dick’s fault—”

7.41.oldText: “A lot I should have cared whose fault it was, if it hurt!” said the young mule.

7.42.oldText: “You must,” said the troop-horse. “If you don’t trust your man, you may as well run away at once. That’s what some of our horses do, and I don’t blame them. As I was saying, it wasn’t Dick’s fault. The man was lying on the ground, and I stretched myself not to tread on him, and he slashed up at me. Next time I have to go over a man lying down I shall step on him—hard.”

7.43.oldText: “Hm!” said Billy. “It sounds very foolish. Knives are dirty things at any time. The proper thing to do is to climb up a mountain with a well-balanced saddle, hang on by all four feet and your ears too, and creep and crawl and wriggle along, till you come out hundreds of feet above anyone else on a ledge where there’s just room enough for your hoofs. Then you stand still and keep quiet—never ask a man to hold your head, young un—keep quiet while the guns are being put together, and then you watch the little poppy shells drop down into the tree-tops ever so far below.”

7.44.oldText: “Don’t you ever trip?” said the troop-horse.

7.45.oldText: “They say that when a mule trips you can split a hen’s ear,” said Billy. “Now and again perhaps a badly packed saddle will upset a mule, but it’s very seldom. I wish I could show you our business. It’s beautiful. Why, it took me three years to find out what the men were driving at. The science of the thing is never to show up against the sky line, because if you do, you may get fired at. Remember that, young un. Always keep hidden as much as possible, even if you have to go a mile out of your way. I lead the battery when it comes to that sort of climbing.”

7.46.oldText: “Fired at without the chance of running into the people who are firing!” said the troop-horse, thinking hard. “I couldn’t stand that. I should want to charge—with Dick.”

7.47.oldText: “Oh, no, you wouldn’t. You know that as soon as the guns are in position they’ll do all the charging. That’s scientific and neat. But knives—pah!”

7.48.oldText: The baggage-camel had been bobbing his head to and fro for some time, anxious to get a word in edgewise. Then I heard him say, as he cleared his throat nervously:

7.49.oldText: “I—I—I have fought a little, but not in that climbing way or that running way.”

7.50.oldText: “No. Now you mention it,” said Billy, “you don’t look as though you were made for climbing or running—much. Well, how was it, old Hay-bales?”

7.51.oldText: “The proper way,” said the camel. “We all sat down—”

7.52.oldText: “Oh, my crupper and breastplate!” said the troop-horse under his breath. “Sat down!”

7.53.oldText: “We sat down—a hundred of us,” the camel went on, “in a big square, and the men piled our packs and saddles outside the square, and they fired over our backs, the men did, on all sides of the square.”

7.54.oldText: “What sort of men? Any men that came along?” said the troop-horse. “They teach us in riding school to lie down and let our masters fire across us, but Dick Cunliffe is the only man I’d trust to do that. It tickles my girths, and besides, I can’t see with my head on the ground.”

7.55.oldText: “What does it matter who fires across you?” said the camel. “There are plenty of men and plenty of other camels close by, and a great many clouds of smoke. I am not frightened then. I sit still and wait.”

7.56.oldText: “And yet,” said Billy, “you dream bad dreams and upset the camp at night. Well, well! Before I’d lie down, not to speak of sitting down, and let a man fire across me, my heels and his head would have something to say to each other. Did you ever hear anything so awful as that?”

7.57.oldText: There was a long silence, and then one of the gun-bullocks lifted up his big head and said, “This is very foolish indeed. There is only one way of fighting.”

7.58.oldText: “Oh, go on,” said Billy. “Please don’t mind me. I suppose you fellows fight standing on your tails?”

7.59.oldText: “Only one way,” said the two together. (They must have been twins.) “This is that way. To put all twenty yoke of us to the big gun as soon as Two Tails trumpets.” (“Two Tails” is camp slang for the elephant.)

7.60.oldText: “What does Two Tails trumpet for?” said the young mule.

7.61.oldText: “To show that he is not going any nearer to the smoke on the other side. Two Tails is a great coward. Then we tug the big gun all together—Heya—Hullah! Heeyah! Hullah! We do not climb like cats nor run like calves. We go across the level plain, twenty yoke of us, till we are unyoked again, and we graze while the big guns talk across the plain to some town with mud walls, and pieces of the wall fall out, and the dust goes up as though many cattle were coming home.”

7.62.oldText: “Oh! And you choose that time for grazing?” said the young mule.

7.63.oldText: “That time or any other. Eating is always good. We eat till we are yoked up again and tug the gun back to where Two Tails is waiting for it. Sometimes there are big guns in the city that speak back, and some of us are killed, and then there is all the more grazing for those that are left. This is Fate. None the less, Two Tails is a great coward. That is the proper way to fight. We are brothers from Hapur. Our father was a sacred bull of Shiva. We have spoken.”

7.64.oldText: “Well, I’ve certainly learned something tonight,” said the troop-horse. “Do you gentlemen of the screw-gun battery feel inclined to eat when you are being fired at with big guns, and Two Tails is behind you?”

7.65.oldText: “About as much as we feel inclined to sit down and let men sprawl all over us, or run into people with knives. I never heard such stuff. A mountain ledge, a well-balanced load, a driver you can trust to let you pick your own way, and I’m your mule. But—the other things—no!” said Billy, with a stamp of his foot.

7.66.oldText: “Of course,” said the troop-horse, “everyone is not made the same way, and I can quite see that your family, on your father’s side, would fail to understand a great many things.”

7.67.oldText: “Never you mind my family on my father’s side,” said Billy angrily, for every mule hates to be reminded that his father was a donkey. “My father was a Southern gentleman, and he could pull down and bite and kick into rags every horse he came across. Remember that, you big brown Brumby!”

7.68.oldText: Brumby means wild horse without any breeding. Imagine the feelings of Sunol if a carthorse called her a “skate,” and you can imagine how the Australian horse felt. I saw the white of his eye glitter in the dark.

7.69.oldText: “See here, you son of an imported Malaga jackass,” he said between his teeth, “I’d have you know that I’m related on my mother’s side to Carbine, winner of the Melbourne Cup, and where I come from we aren’t used to being ridden over roughshod by any parrot-mouthed, pig-headed mule in a pop-gun pea-shooter battery. Are you ready?”

7.70.oldText: “On your hind legs!” squealed Billy. They both reared up facing each other, and I was expecting a furious fight, when a gurgly, rumbly voice called out of the darkness to the right—“Children, what are you fighting about there? Be quiet.”

7.71.oldText: Both beasts dropped down with a snort of disgust, for neither horse nor mule can bear to listen to an elephant’s voice.

7.72.oldText: “It’s Two Tails!” said the troop-horse. “I can’t stand him. A tail at each end isn’t fair!”

7.73.oldText: “My feelings exactly,” said Billy, crowding into the troop-horse for company. “We’re very alike in some things.”

7.74.oldText: “I suppose we’ve inherited them from our mothers,” said the troop-horse. “It’s not worth quarreling about. Hi! Two Tails, are you tied up?”

7.75.oldText: “Yes,” said Two Tails, with a laugh all up his trunk. “I’m picketed for the night. I’ve heard what you fellows have been saying. But don’t be afraid. I’m not coming over.”

7.76.oldText: The bullocks and the camel said, half aloud, “Afraid of Two Tails—what nonsense!” And the bullocks went on, “We are sorry that you heard, but it is true. Two Tails, why are you afraid of the guns when they fire?”

7.77.oldText: “Well,” said Two Tails, rubbing one hind leg against the other, exactly like a little boy reciting a poem, “I don’t quite know whether you’d understand.”

7.78.oldText: “We don’t, but we have to pull the guns,” said the bullocks.

7.79.oldText: “I know it, and I know you are a good deal braver than you think you are. But it’s different with me. My battery captain called me a Pachydermatous Anachronism the other day.”

7.80.oldText: “That’s another way of fighting, I suppose?” said Billy, who was recovering his spirits.

7.81.oldText: “You don’t know what that means, of course, but I do. It means betwixt and between, and that is just where I am. I can see inside my head what will happen when a shell bursts, and you bullocks can’t.”

7.82.oldText: “I can,” said the troop-horse. “At least a little bit. I try not to think about it.”

7.83.oldText: “I can see more than you, and I do think about it. I know there’s a great deal of me to take care of, and I know that nobody knows how to cure me when I’m sick. All they can do is to stop my driver’s pay till I get well, and I can’t trust my driver.”

7.84.oldText: “Ah!” said the troop-horse. “That explains it. I can trust Dick.”

7.85.oldText: “You could put a whole regiment of Dicks on my back without making me feel any better. I know just enough to be uncomfortable, and not enough to go on in spite of it.”

7.86.oldText: “We do not understand,” said the bullocks.

7.87.oldText: “I know you don’t. I’m not talking to you. You don’t know what blood is.”

7.88.oldText: “We do,” said the bullocks. “It is red stuff that soaks into the ground and smells.”

7.89.oldText: The troop-horse gave a kick and a bound and a snort.

7.90.oldText: “Don’t talk of it,” he said. “I can smell it now, just thinking of it. It makes me want to run—when I haven’t Dick on my back.”

7.91.oldText: “But it is not here,” said the camel and the bullocks. “Why are you so stupid?”

7.92.oldText: “It’s vile stuff,” said Billy. “I don’t want to run, but I don’t want to talk about it.”

7.93.oldText: “There you are!” said Two Tails, waving his tail to explain.

7.94.oldText: “Surely. Yes, we have been here all night,” said the bullocks.

7.95.oldText: Two Tails stamped his foot till the iron ring on it jingled. “Oh, I’m not talking to you. You can’t see inside your heads.”

7.96.oldText: “No. We see out of our four eyes,” said the bullocks. “We see straight in front of us.”

7.97.oldText: “If I could do that and nothing else, you wouldn’t be needed to pull the big guns at all. If I was like my captain—he can see things inside his head before the firing begins, and he shakes all over, but he knows too much to run away—if I was like him I could pull the guns. But if I were as wise as all that I should never be here. I should be a king in the forest, as I used to be, sleeping half the day and bathing when I liked. I haven’t had a good bath for a month.”

7.98.oldText: “That’s all very fine,” said Billy. “But giving a thing a long name doesn’t make it any better.”

7.99.oldText: “Hush!” said the troop-horse. “I think I understand what Two Tails means.”

7.100.oldText: “You’ll understand better in a minute,” said Two Tails angrily. “Now you just explain to me why you don’t like this!”

7.101.oldText: He began trumpeting furiously at the top of his trumpet.

7.102.oldText: “Stop that!” said Billy and the troop-horse together, and I could hear them stamp and shiver. An elephant’s trumpeting is always nasty, especially on a dark night.

7.103.oldText: “I shan’t stop,” said Two Tails. “Won’t you explain that, please? Hhrrmph! Rrrt! Rrrmph! Rrrhha!” Then he stopped suddenly, and I heard a little whimper in the dark, and knew that Vixen had found me at last. She knew as well as I did that if there is one thing in the world the elephant is more afraid of than another it is a little barking dog. So she stopped to bully Two Tails in his pickets, and yapped round his big feet. Two Tails shuffled and squeaked. “Go away, little dog!” he said. “Don’t snuff at my ankles, or I’ll kick at you. Good little dog—nice little doggie, then! Go home, you yelping little beast! Oh, why doesn’t someone take her away? She’ll bite me in a minute.”

7.104.oldText: “Seems to me,” said Billy to the troop-horse, “that our friend Two Tails is afraid of most things. Now, if I had a full meal for every dog I’ve kicked across the parade-ground I should be nearly as fat as Two Tails.”

7.105.oldText: I whistled, and Vixen ran up to me, muddy all over, and licked my nose, and told me a long tale about hunting for me all through the camp. I never let her know that I understood beast talk, or she would have taken all sorts of liberties. So I buttoned her into the breast of my overcoat, and Two Tails shuffled and stamped and growled to himself.

7.106.oldText: “Extraordinary! Most extraordinary!” he said. “It runs in our family. Now, where has that nasty little beast gone to?”

7.107.oldText: I heard him feeling about with his trunk.

7.108.oldText: “We all seem to be affected in various ways,” he went on, blowing his nose. “Now, you gentlemen were alarmed, I believe, when I trumpeted.”

7.109.oldText: “Not alarmed, exactly,” said the troop-horse, “but it made me feel as though I had hornets where my saddle ought to be. Don’t begin again.”

7.110.oldText: “I’m frightened of a little dog, and the camel here is frightened by bad dreams in the night.”

7.111.oldText: “It is very lucky for us that we haven’t all got to fight in the same way,” said the troop-horse.

7.112.oldText: “What I want to know,” said the young mule, who had been quiet for a long time—“what I want to know is, why we have to fight at all.”

7.113.oldText: “Because we’re told to,” said the troop-horse, with a snort of contempt.

7.114.oldText: “Orders,” said Billy the mule, and his teeth snapped.

7.115.oldText: “Hukm hai!” (It is an order!), said the camel with a gurgle, and Two Tails and the bullocks repeated, “Hukm hai!”

7.116.oldText: “Yes, but who gives the orders?” said the recruit-mule.

7.117.oldText: “The man who walks at your head—or sits on your back—or holds the nose rope—or twists your tail,” said Billy and the troop-horse and the camel and the bullocks one after the other.

7.119.oldText: “Now you want to know too much, young un,” said Billy, “and that is one way of getting kicked. All you have to do is to obey the man at your head and ask no questions.”

7.120.oldText: “He’s quite right,” said Two Tails. “I can’t always obey, because I’m betwixt and between. But Billy’s right. Obey the man next to you who gives the order, or you’ll stop all the battery, besides getting a thrashing.”

7.121.oldText: The gun-bullocks got up to go. “Morning is coming,” they said. “We will go back to our lines. It is true that we only see out of our eyes, and we are not very clever. But still, we are the only people tonight who have not been afraid. Good-night, you brave people.”

7.122.oldText: Nobody answered, and the troop-horse said, to change the conversation, “Where’s that little dog? A dog means a man somewhere about.”

7.123.oldText: “Here I am,” yapped Vixen, “under the gun tail with my man. You big, blundering beast of a camel, you upset our tent. My man’s very angry.”

7.124.oldText: “Phew!” said the bullocks. “He must be white!”

7.125.oldText: “Of course he is,” said Vixen. “Do you suppose I’m looked after by a black bullock-driver?”

7.126.oldText: “Huah! Ouach! Ugh!” said the bullocks. “Let us get away quickly.”

7.127.oldText: They plunged forward in the mud, and managed somehow to run their yoke onto the pole of an ammunition wagon, where it jammed.

7.128.oldText: “Now you have done it,” said Billy calmly. “Don’t struggle. You’re hung up till daylight. What on earth’s the matter?”

7.129.oldText: The bullocks went off into the long hissing snorts that Indian cattle give, and pushed and crowded and slewed and stamped and slipped and nearly fell down in the mud, grunting savagely.

7.130.oldText: “You’ll break your necks in a minute,” said the troop-horse. “What’s the matter with white men? I live with them.”

7.131.oldText: “They—eat—us! Pull!” said the near bullock. The yoke snapped with a twang, and they lumbered off together.

7.132.oldText: I never knew before what made Indian cattle so scared of Englishmen. We eat beef—a thing that no cattle-driver touches—and of course the cattle do not like it.

7.133.oldText: “May I be flogged with my own pad-chains! Who’d have thought of two big lumps like those losing their heads?” said Billy.

7.134.oldText: “Never mind. I’m going to look at this man. Most of the white men, I know, have things in their pockets,” said the troop-horse.

7.135.oldText: “I’ll leave you, then. I can’t say I’m over-fond of them myself. Besides, white men who haven’t a place to sleep in are more than likely to be thieves, and I’ve a good deal of Government property on my back. Come along, young un, and we’ll go back to our lines. Good-night, Australia! See you on parade tomorrow, I suppose. Good-night, old Hay-bale!—try to control your feelings, won’t you? Good-night, Two Tails! If you pass us on the ground tomorrow, don’t trumpet. It spoils our formation.”

7.136.oldText: Billy the Mule stumped off with the swaggering limp of an old campaigner, as the troop-horse’s head came nuzzling into my breast, and I gave him biscuits, while Vixen, who is a most conceited little dog, told him fibs about the scores of horses that she and I kept.

7.137.oldText: “I’m coming to the parade tomorrow in my dog-cart,” she said. “Where will you be?”

7.138.oldText: “On the left hand of the second squadron. I set the time for all my troop, little lady,” he said politely. “Now I must go back to Dick. My tail’s all muddy, and he’ll have two hours’ hard work dressing me for parade.”

7.139.oldText: The big parade of all the thirty thousand men was held that afternoon, and Vixen and I had a good place close to the Viceroy and the Amir of Afghanistan, with his high, big black hat of astrakhan wool and the great diamond star in the center. The first part of the review was all sunshine, and the regiments went by in wave upon wave of legs all moving together, and guns all in a line, till our eyes grew dizzy. Then the cavalry came up, to the beautiful cavalry canter of “Bonnie Dundee,” and Vixen cocked her ear where she sat on the dog-cart. The second squadron of the Lancers shot by, and there was the troop-horse, with his tail like spun silk, his head pulled into his breast, one ear forward and one back, setting the time for all his squadron, his legs going as smoothly as waltz music. Then the big guns came by, and I saw Two Tails and two other elephants harnessed in line to a forty-pounder siege gun, while twenty yoke of oxen walked behind. The seventh pair had a new yoke, and they looked rather stiff and tired. Last came the screw guns, and Billy the mule carried himself as though he commanded all the troops, and his harness was oiled and polished till it winked. I gave a cheer all by myself for Billy the mule, but he never looked right or left.

7.140.oldText: The rain began to fall again, and for a while it was too misty to see what the troops were doing. They had made a big half circle across the plain, and were spreading out into a line. That line grew and grew and grew till it was three-quarters of a mile long from wing to wing—one solid wall of men, horses, and guns. Then it came on straight toward the Viceroy and the Amir, and as it got nearer the ground began to shake, like the deck of a steamer when the engines are going fast.

7.141.oldText: Unless you have been there you cannot imagine what a frightening effect this steady advance of troops has on the spectators, even when they know it is only a review. I looked at the Amir. Up till then he had not shown the shadow of a sign of astonishment or anything else. But now his eyes began to get bigger and bigger, and he picked up the reins on his horse’s neck and looked behind him. For a minute it seemed as though he were going to draw his sword and slash his way out through the English men and women in the carriages at the back. Then the advance stopped dead, the ground stood still, the whole line saluted, and thirty bands began to play all together. That was the end of the review, and the regiments went off to their camps in the rain, and an infantry band struck up with—

7.142.oldText:
The animals went in two by two,
     Hurrah!
The animals went in two by two,
The elephant and the battery mul’,
and they all got into the Ark
     For to get out of the rain!

7.143.oldText: Then I heard an old grizzled, long-haired Central Asian chief, who had come down with the Amir, asking questions of a native officer.

7.144.oldText: “Now,” said he, “in what manner was this wonderful thing done?”

7.145.oldText: And the officer answered, “An order was given, and they obeyed.”

7.146.oldText: “But are the beasts as wise as the men?” said the chief.

7.147.oldText: “They obey, as the men do. Mule, horse, elephant, or bullock, he obeys his driver, and the driver his sergeant, and the sergeant his lieutenant, and the lieutenant his captain, and the captain his major, and the major his colonel, and the colonel his brigadier commanding three regiments, and the brigadier the general, who obeys the Viceroy, who is the servant of the Empress. Thus it is done.”

7.148.oldText: “Would it were so in Afghanistan!” said the chief, “for there we obey only our own wills.”

7.149.oldText: “And for that reason,” said the native officer, twirling his mustache, “your Amir whom you do not obey must come here and take orders from our Viceroy.”

7.152.oldText:
We lent to Alexander the strength of Hercules,
The wisdom of our foreheads, the cunning of our knees;
We bowed our necks to service: they ne’er were loosed again,—
Make way there—way for the ten-foot teams
      Of the Forty-Pounder train!

7.154.oldText:
Those heroes in their harnesses avoid a cannon-ball,
And what they know of powder upsets them one and all;
Then we come into action and tug the guns again—
Make way there—way for the twenty yoke
      Of the Forty-Pounder train!

7.156.oldText:
By the brand on my shoulder, the finest of tunes
Is played by the Lancers, Hussars, and Dragoons,
And it’s sweeter than “Stables” or “Water” to me—
The Cavalry Canter of “Bonnie Dundee”!

7.157.oldText:
Then feed us and break us and handle and groom,
And give us good riders and plenty of room,
And launch us in column of squadron and see
The way of the war-horse to “Bonnie Dundee”!

7.159.oldText:
As me and my companions were scrambling up a hill,
The path was lost in rolling stones, but we went forward still;
For we can wriggle and climb, my lads, and turn up everywhere,
Oh, it’s our delight on a mountain height, with a leg or two to
   spare!

7.160.oldText:
Good luck to every sergeant, then, that lets us pick our road;
Bad luck to all the driver-men that cannot pack a load:
For we can wriggle and climb, my lads, and turn up everywhere,
Oh, it’s our delight on a mountain height, with a leg or two to
   spare!

7.162.oldText:
We haven’t a camelty tune of our own
To help us trollop along,
But every neck is a hair trombone
(_Rtt-ta-ta-ta!_ is a hair trombone!)
And this our marching-song:
_Can’t!  Don’t!  Sha’n’t!  Won’t!_
Pass it along the line!
Somebody’s pack has slid from his back,
Wish it were only mine!
Somebody’s load has tipped off in the road—
Cheer for a halt and a row!
_Urrr!  Yarrh!  Grr!  Arrh!_
Somebody’s catching it now!

7.164.oldText:
Children of the Camp are we,
Serving each in his degree;
Children of the yoke and goad,
Pack and harness, pad and load.
See our line across the plain,
Like a heel-rope bent again,
Reaching, writhing, rolling far,
Sweeping all away to war!
While the men that walk beside,
Dusty, silent, heavy-eyed,
Cannot tell why we or they
March and suffer day by day.
   _Children of the Camp are we,
   Serving each in his degree;
   Children of the yoke and goad,
   Pack and harness, pad and load!_

1.0.oldText:
Nu bringer Rann Glenten natten hjem,
som Mang Flagermusen slipper fri —
hjordene er lukket inde i stalde og hytter,
mens vi er frie til daggry.
Dette er stolthedens og magtens time,
klo og hugtand og pote.
Åh, hør kaldet! — God jagt til alle,
der følger Junglens Lov!
_Natsang i Junglen_

1.4.oldText: »Ikke for en ulv,« sagde Tabaqui, »men for en så ydmyg en som mig er et tørt ben et fint festmåltid. Hvem er vi, Gidur-log [sjakalfolket], til at være kræsne?« Han skyndte sig om bag i hulen, hvor han fandt benet af en buk med lidt kød på, og satte sig tilfreds og knasede i enden af det.

1.5.oldText: »Tak for dette gode måltid,« sagde han og slikkede sig om munden. »Hvor smukke de ædle børn er! Hvor er deres øjne store! Og så unge! Sandelig, sandelig, jeg burde have husket, at kongebørn er mænd fra fødslen.«

1.6.oldText: Tabaqui vidste lige så godt som alle andre, at intet bringer så meget uheld som at rose børn lige op i ansigtet. Det fornøjede ham at se, hvor ubehageligt det var for Mor og Far Ulv.

1.7.oldText: Tabaqui sad stille og frydede sig over ulykken, han havde anrettet, og så sagde han ondskabsfuldt:

1.11.oldText: »Der er en grund til, at hans mor kaldte ham Lungri [Den Halte],« sagde Mor Ulv stille. »Han har været halt i den ene fod, siden han blev født. Det er derfor, han kun har dræbt kvæg. Nu er landsbyfolkene ved Waingunga vrede på ham, og så er han kommet hertil for at gøre vores landsbyfolk vrede. Længe efter at han er rejst, vil de lede efter ham i junglen, og når de sætter ild til græsset, må vi og vores børn flygte. Ja, vi skylder virkelig Shere Khan stor tak!«

1.17.oldText: »Sssh. Det er hverken tyr eller buk, han jager i nat,« sagde Mor Ulv. »Det er Menneske.«

1.18.oldText: Klynken blev til en slags hummende spinden, der lød, som om den kom fra alle sider på én gang. Den lyd forvirrer skovhuggere og sigøjnere, der sover udendørs, så de nogle gange render lige ind i gabet på tigeren.

1.20.oldText: Junglens Lov befaler aldrig noget uden grund. Den forbyder ethvert dyr at æde Menneske, medmindre det dræber for at lære sine unger, hvordan man gør; og selv da skal det jage uden for sin flok eller stammes jagtmarker. Den egentlige grund er, at når man dræber et menneske, kommer der før eller siden hvide mænd på elefanter med geværer, og hundredvis af brune mænd med gonger, raketter og fakler. Så lider alle i junglen. Dyrene fortæller hinanden, at Menneske er det svageste og mest forsvarsløse af alle levende væsener, så det er ikke fair jagt at røre ham. De siger også — og det er sandt — at menneskeædere får fnat og mister tænderne.

1.22.oldText: Så udstødte Shere Khan et hyl — et hyl, der slet ikke lød som en tiger. »Han missede,« sagde Mor Ulv. »Hvad er der sket?«

1.35.oldText: »Mit bytte. Et menneskebarn løb denne vej,« sagde Shere Khan. »Dets forældre er stukket af. Giv det til mig.«

1.39.oldText: Tigerens brøl fyldte hulen med torden. Mor Ulv rystede sig fri af hvalpene og sprang frem, hendes øjne som to grønne måner i mørket vendt mod Shere Khans flammende øjne.

1.41.oldText: Far Ulv så forbløffet til. Han havde næsten glemt den gang, han vandt Mor Ulv i åben kamp mod fem andre ulve, dengang hun løb med Flokken, og navnet Dæmonen ikke bare var pæne ord. Shere Khan kunne måske have holdt stand mod Far Ulv, men mod Mor Ulv kunne han ikke gøre noget. Han vidste, at hun stod stærkt, hvor hun stod, og at hun ville kæmpe til døden. Snerrende bakkede han ud af hulen, og da han var kommet udenfor, råbte han:

1.43.oldText: Mor Ulv kastede sig udmattet ned blandt hvalpene, og Far Ulv sagde alvorligt til hende:

1.51.oldText: Der steg dybe knurren op overalt. En ung ulv på sit fjerde år kastede Shere Khans spørgsmål tilbage mod Akela: »Hvad har det Frie Folk med et menneskebarn at gøre?« Junglens Lov siger nemlig, at hvis nogen bestrider en hvalps ret til at blive optaget i Flokken, skal mindst to af Flokkens medlemmer tale hans sag, og ingen af dem må være hans far eller mor.

1.52.oldText: »Hvem vil tale for denne unge?« spurgte Akela. »Hvem af det Frie Folk vil tale?« Ingen svarede. Mor Ulv gjorde sig klar til en kamp, som, vidste hun, ville blive hendes sidste, hvis det kom til kamp.

1.54.oldText: »Et menneskebarn — et menneskebarn?« sagde han. »Jeg vil tale for menneskebarnet. Et menneskebarn kan ikke gøre nogen skade. Jeg er ingen stor taler, men det, jeg siger, er sandt. Lad ham løbe med Flokken og blive optaget sammen med de andre. Jeg vil selv lære ham op.«

1.55.oldText: »Vi mangler endnu én stemme,« sagde Akela. »Baloo, som underviser vores unge hvalpe, har talt for ham. Hvem andre vil tale efter Baloo?«

1.61.oldText: »At dræbe en forsvarsløs, nøgen unge er en skam. Og når han bliver voksen, kan han måske give jer bedre jagt. Baloo har talt for ham. Til Baloos ord vil jeg lægge en tyr — en fed tyr, nydræbt, mindre end en halv engelsk mil herfra — hvis I vil tage imod menneskebarnet efter Loven. Er det så svært?«

1.64.oldText: »Ja, brøl du bare,« mumlede Bagheera i sine knurhår. »For hvis jeg ellers kender noget til mennesker, kommer der en dag, hvor denne nøgne lille skabning får dig til at brøle om noget helt andet.«

1.66.oldText: »Sandelig til nytte, når der er brug for hjælp. Ingen kan regne med at være Flokkens leder for evigt,« sagde Bagheera.

1.68.oldText: »Tag ham med,« sagde han til Far Ulv, »og oplær ham, som det sømmer sig for én af det Frie Folk.«

1.69.oldText: Og sådan blev Mowgli medlem af Seeonees Ulveflok, købt med en tyr og på Baloos ord.

1.70.oldText: Nu må du lade ti eller elleve hele år gå og selv forestille dig det vidunderlige liv, Mowgli levede blandt ulvene. At fortælle det hele ville fylde utallige bøger. Han voksede op sammen med hvalpene, selv om de naturligvis var voksne ulve, næsten før han var kommet ud af barndommen. Far Ulv lærte ham alt, hvad han skulle vide, og viste ham, hvad tingene i junglen betød. Snart sagde en raslen i græsset, et pust af varm natteluft, et ugleråb over hovedet, skrabet fra en flagermus' kløer, når den satte sig i et træ for at hvile, eller plasket fra en lille fisk, der sprang i en pøl, lige så meget til ham, som arbejdet på kontoret siger til en forretningsmand. Når han ikke lærte noget, lå han i solen og sov, spiste og faldt i søvn igen. Når han var varm eller snavset, svømmede han i skovens vandhuller. Og når han ville have honning (Baloo havde fortalt ham, at honning og nødder smagte lige så godt som råt kød), klatrede han op efter den, og Bagheera havde vist ham, hvordan man gør. Bagheera lagde sig ud på en gren og kaldte: »Kom så, Lillebror.« Først klamrede Mowgli sig til træet som et dovendyr, men senere kastede han sig fra gren til gren næsten lige så frygtløst som den grå abe. Han havde også sin plads på Rådsklippen, når Flokken mødtes. Dér opdagede han, at hvis han stirrede hårdt på en ulv, måtte ulven slå blikket ned. Så han begyndte at stirre på dem for sjov. Andre gange trak han lange torne ud af sine venners poteballer, for ulve lider meget under torne og burrer i pelsen. Om natten gik han ned ad bakken til de dyrkede marker og kiggede meget nysgerrigt på landsbyboerne i deres hytter, men han stolede ikke på mennesker. Bagheera havde engang vist ham en firkantet kasse med en faldlåge, så snedigt gemt i junglen, at han næsten var trådt ind i den, og havde fortalt ham, at det var en fælde. Mest af alt elskede Mowgli at gå sammen med Bagheera dybt ind i den varme, mørke skov, sove hele den søvnige dag og om natten se Bagheera dræbe. Når Bagheera var sulten, dræbte han, hvad der kom i vejen, og det gjorde Mowgli også — med én undtagelse. Så snart drengen kunne forstå det, fortalte Bagheera ham, at han aldrig måtte røre kvæg, fordi han var blevet købt ind i Flokken med en tyrs liv. »Hele junglen er din,« sagde Bagheera, »og du kan dræbe alt, hvad du er stærk nok til. Men husk tyren, der købte din plads: du må aldrig dræbe eller spise kvæg, hverken ungt eller gammelt. Det er Junglens Lov.« Mowgli holdt trofast den regel.

1.75.oldText: En meget varm dag fik Bagheera en ny tanke, efter noget han havde hørt. Måske var nyheden kommet fra Ikki Pindsvinet. Dybt inde i junglen, mens drengen lå med hovedet på panterens smukke sorte pels, sagde Bagheera: »Lillebror, hvor mange gange har jeg advaret dig om, at Shere Khan er din fjende?«

1.78.oldText: »Ha! Ha!« sagde Mowgli. »Tabaqui kom til mig for ikke længe siden med noget uforskammet snak om, at jeg var et nøgent menneskebarn og ikke duede til at grave svinerødder op. Men jeg greb Tabaqui i halen og svingede ham to gange mod et palmetræ for at lære ham bedre manerer.«

1.81.oldText: Bagheera strakte sig helt ud og lod øjenlågene synke. »Lillebror,« sagde han, »læg din hånd under min kæbe.«

1.83.oldText: »Ingen i junglen ved, at jeg, Bagheera, bærer det mærke — mærket efter et halsbånd. Men jeg blev født blandt mennesker, Lillebror, og blandt mennesker døde min mor, i burene i kongens palads i Oodeypore. Det var derfor, jeg betalte for dit liv ved Rådet, da du var en lille nøgen unge. Ja, også jeg er født blandt mennesker. Jeg havde aldrig set junglen. Bag tremmer fik jeg mad i en jernskål. Så en nat følte jeg, at jeg var Bagheera — Panteren — og ikke noget menneskes legetøj. Med ét slag af poten smadrede jeg deres latterlige lås og gik min vej. Fordi jeg kendte menneskenes måder, blev jeg mere frygtet i junglen end Shere Khan. Er det ikke sandt?«

1.85.oldText: »Åh, du er et menneskebarn,« sagde den Sorte Panter meget kærligt. »Og lige som jeg vendte tilbage til min jungle, sådan må du vende tilbage til menneskene til sidst — til de mennesker, der er dine brødre — hvis du ikke bliver dræbt på Rådet.«

1.89.oldText: »Ingen har fortalt mig noget af det her,« sagde Mowgli surt, og hans tykke sorte øjenbryn trak sig sammen i en rynke.

1.95.oldText: »Ved den Brækkede Lås, der gav mig fri, er jeg sikker, Lillebror.«

1.100.oldText: »Bare noget flagermusesnak om Shere Khan,« råbte han tilbage. »I nat jager jeg nede på de pløjede marker.« Han styrtede gennem buskene mod åen i dalbunden. Dér standsede han brat. Flokkens jagtråb lød, og så brølet fra en sambarhjort, de forfulgte, og en snorken, da bukken vendte sig for at forsvare sig. De unge ulve brød ud i grusomme, hånlige hyl: »Akela! Akela! Lad os se Den Ensomme Ulvs styrke. Plads til Flokkens leder! Spring, Akela!«

1.104.oldText: Han løftede ansigtet op til vinduet for at se ilden brænde på arnen. I løbet af natten så han bondens kone rejse sig og lægge sorte klumper på den. Da morgenen kom med kold, hvid tåge, så han mandens barn tage en flettet krukke, der var beklædt indvendigt med ler. Barnet fyldte den med stykker af glødende trækul, puttede den ind under sit tæppe og gik ud for at passe køerne i stalden.

1.106.oldText: »De ligner mig meget,« sagde Mowgli og blæste ind i krukken, som han havde set konen gøre. »Hvis jeg ikke giver den noget at æde, dør den her.« Han lagde tør bark og kviste på de glødende kul. Halvvejs oppe ad bakken mødte han Bagheera, med morgendug, der glimtede som månesten i hans pels.

1.115.oldText: »Da jeg ser, at lederskabet stadig er åbent, og da jeg er blevet bedt om at tale—« begyndte Shere Khan.

1.116.oldText: »Af hvem?« krævede Mowgli. »Er vi alle blevet sjakaler, der logrer for denne kvægslagter? Det er kun Flokken, der bestemmer, hvem der skal lede Flokken.«

1.119.oldText: »Frie Folk — og I også, Shere Khans sjakaler — i tolv sæsoner har jeg ført jer ud på jagt og hjem igen. I alle de år er ikke én af jer blevet fanget i en fælde eller gjort til krøbling. Nu har jeg ikke fået mit bytte. I ved, hvem der planlagde det, og hvordan. I ved, at I sendte mig mod en buk, hvis styrke jeg ikke kendte, for at afsløre min svaghed. Det var en snedig list. I har ret til at dræbe mig her, nu, på Rådsklippen. Derfor spørger jeg: Hvem træder frem og gør en ende på Den Ensomme Ulv? For efter Junglens Lov har jeg ret til, at I kommer én ad gangen.«

1.120.oldText: Der var længe stille, for ingen af ulvene ville kæmpe på liv og død mod Akela alene. Til sidst brølede Shere Khan: »Pyt! Hvorfor bekymre os om denne tandløse tåbe? Han skal alligevel dø! Det er menneskebarnet, der har levet for længe. Frie Folk, han var mit bytte fra begyndelsen. Giv ham til mig. Jeg er træt af al den sludder om, at et menneske kan være en ulv. I ti sæsoner har han forstyrret junglen. Udlever menneskebarnet, ellers jager jeg her for evigt og efterlader ikke så meget som ét ben til jer. Han er et menneske, et menneskes barn, og jeg hader ham helt ind i knoglemarven!«

1.129.oldText: »Et menneske — et menneske — det er det, han er!« snerrede ulvene. De fleste begyndte at samle sig om Shere Khan, hvis hale var begyndt at piske.

1.131.oldText: Mowgli rejste sig i sin fulde højde med ildkrukken i hænderne. Han strakte armene ud og gabede lige op i ansigtet på Rådet, selv om raseri og sorg brændte i ham. Ulvene havde nemlig, som ulve gør, aldrig ladet ham mærke, at de hadede ham. »Hør nu efter!« råbte han. »Nu er det slut med at gø som hunde. I har sagt så mange gange i nat, at jeg er et menneske — selv om jeg gerne ville have været ulv hos jer hele mit liv — at jeg føler, I må have ret. Så jeg kalder jer ikke længere mine brødre. Jeg kalder jer sag [hunde], som et menneske bør. Det er ikke op til jer, hvad I vil eller ikke vil gøre. Det bestemmer jeg. For at gøre det helt tydeligt har jeg, mennesket, hentet lidt af den Røde Blomst, som I hunde er bange for.«

1.138.oldText: »Denne kvægslagter sagde, at han ville dræbe mig her på Rådet, fordi han ikke fik dræbt mig, da jeg var en unge. Nå, sådan slår mennesker hunde — sådan her og sådan her. Rør et eneste knurhår, Lungri, og jeg propper den Røde Blomst ned i halsen på dig!« Han slog Shere Khan i hovedet med grenen. I ren pinsel af skræk klynkede og hvinede tigeren.

1.140.oldText: »Hvad er det? Hvad er det?« sagde han. »Jeg ønsker ikke at forlade junglen, og jeg ved ikke, hvad dette er. Er jeg ved at dø, Bagheera?«

1.150.oldText:
Da daggryet brød frem, kaldte sambarhjorten
én, to, og atter en gang!
Og en hind sprang op, og en hind sprang op
fra vandhullet i skoven, hvor de vilde hjorte drikker.
Dette så jeg, da jeg spejdede alene,
én, to, og atter en gang!

1.151.oldText:
Da daggryet brød frem, brølede sambarhjorten
én, to, og atter en gang!
Og en ulv listede tilbage, og en ulv listede tilbage
for at bringe ordet til den ventende flok,
og vi søgte, og vi fandt, og vi gøede i hans spor
én, to, og atter en gang!

1.152.oldText:
Da daggryet brød frem, hylede Ulveflokken
én, to, og atter en gang!
Fødder i junglen, der ikke efterlader spor!

1.153.oldText:
Øjne der kan se i mørket — mørket!
Råb — råb ad det! Hør! Åh, hør!
én, to, og atter en gang!

2.0.oldText: Hans pletter er Leopardens glæde; hans horn er Bøffelens stolthed. Hold dig ren, for en jægers styrke kan ses på pelsens glans. Hvis du opdager, at Tyren kan kaste dig op i luften, eller at den tunge sambarhjort med de tykke bryn kan stange dig, så behøver du ikke afbryde arbejdet for at fortælle os det: vi vidste det allerede for ti årstider siden.

2.1.oldText:
Plag ikke den fremmedes unger, men hils dem som Søster og Broder,
for selv om de er små og buttede, kan det være, at Bjørnen er deres mor.
»Der findes ingen som mig!« siger Ungen i sin stolthed over sit første drab;
men junglen er stor, og Ungen er lille. Lad ham tænke efter og tie stille.
_Baloos leveregler_

2.2.oldText: Alt det, der fortælles her, skete, før Mowgli blev jaget ud af Seeonee-ulveflokken, og før han tog hævn over tigeren Shere Khan. Dengang lærte Baloo ham stadig Junglens Lov. Den store, alvorlige, gamle brune bjørn var glad for at have en så lærenem elev. De unge ulve lærer nemlig kun den del af Junglens Lov, der handler om deres egen flok og stamme, og de løber deres vej, så snart de kan remse Jagtverset op: »Fødder, der går uden lyd; øjne, der ser i mørke; ører, der kan høre vindene i deres huler; og skarpe hvide tænder — det er kendetegnene på alle vore brødre, undtagen Tabaqui Sjakalen og Hyænen, som vi hader.« Men Mowgli var en menneskeunge og måtte lære langt mere. Nogle gange kom den sorte panter Bagheera slentrende gennem junglen for at se, hvordan hans yndling klarede sig. Han lagde hovedet mod et træ og spandt, mens Mowgli sagde dagens lektie op for Baloo. Drengen kunne nu klatre næsten lige så godt, som han kunne svømme, og svømme næsten lige så godt, som han kunne løbe. Derfor lærte Baloo, Lovens Lærer, ham også Skovens og Vandets Love. Han lærte at kende forskel på rådne grene og stærke, at tale høfligt til de vilde bier, når han fandt en bikube halvtreds fod oppe i et træ, at sige det rigtige til flagermusen Mang, hvis han forstyrrede ham i grenene midt på dagen, og at advare vandslangerne, før han plumpede ned i deres vandhuller. Ingen af Junglens Folk bryder sig om at blive forstyrret, og enhver af dem går straks til angreb mod en ubuden gæst. Mowgli lærte også Fremmedes Jagtråb. Hver gang en af Junglens Folk jager uden for sit eget område, skal han råbe det højt og blive ved, indtil nogen svarer. Oversat betyder det: »Giv mig lov at jage her, for jeg er sulten.« Og svaret er: »Jag da for at få mad, men ikke for sjov.«

2.6.oldText: »Blidt!« knurrede Bagheera. »Hvad ved du om at være blid, gamle Jernfod? Hans ansigt er fuldt af blå mærker i dag på grund af din — blidhed. Uf.«

2.14.oldText: »Vi er af ét blod, du og jeg,« sagde Mowgli og talte med den bjørneagtige accent, som alle i Jagtfolket har.

2.25.oldText: »Whuf!« Med den ene store pote fejede Baloo Mowgli af Bagheeras ryg. Som drengen lå mellem de enorme forpoter, kunne han se, at Bjørnen var vred.

2.29.oldText: »Da Baloo gjorde ondt i mit hoved,« sagde Mowgli, som stadig lå på ryggen, »gik jeg min vej. De grå aber kom ned fra træerne og havde ondt af mig. Ingen andre brød sig om det.« Han snøftede lidt.

2.30.oldText: »Abefolkets medfølelse!« fnyste Baloo. »Så fredfyldt som en bjergbæk! Så kølig som sommersolen! Og hvad så, menneskeunge?«

2.33.oldText: »De var meget venlige og bad mig komme igen. Hvorfor er jeg aldrig blevet bragt blandt Abefolket? De står på deres fødder ligesom jeg. De slår mig ikke med deres hårde poter. De leger hele dagen. Lad mig komme op! Slemme Baloo, lad mig op! Jeg vil lege med dem igen.«

2.34.oldText: »Hør efter, menneskeunge,« sagde Bjørnen, og hans stemme rumlede som torden på en lummer nat. »Jeg har lært dig hele Junglens Lov for alle junglens folk — undtagen Abefolket oppe i træerne. De har slet ingen lov. De er udstødte. De har intet eget sprog, men stjæler de ord, de opsnapper, når de sidder højt oppe i grenene og lytter og kigger ned. Deres veje er ikke vores veje. De har ingen ledere. De husker ingenting. De praler og pludrer og lader, som om de er et mægtigt folk, der lige er ved at udrette store ting i junglen. Så falder en nød ned, de begynder at le, og så er alt glemt. Vi i junglen vil ikke have noget med dem at gøre. Vi drikker ikke, hvor aberne drikker, og vi går ikke, hvor aberne går. Vi jager ikke, hvor de jager, og vi dør ikke, hvor de dør. Har du før i dag nogensinde hørt mig tale om Bandar-log?«

2.36.oldText: »Junglens Folk lader dem ude af mund og sind. De er meget mange, onde, beskidte, skamløse, og de ønsker, hvis de overhovedet har noget fast ønske, at blive bemærket af Junglens Folk. Men vi bemærker dem ikke, selv når de kaster nødder og snavs på vore hoveder.«

2.40.oldText: »Jeg — jeg? Hvordan skulle jeg gætte, at han ville lege med sådant skidt. Abefolket! Føj!«

2.41.oldText: Endnu et regnskyl faldt ned over deres hoveder. De to dyr travede af sted med Mowgli imellem sig. Alt, hvad Baloo havde sagt om aberne, var sandt. De boede i trætoppene, og da dyr sjældent ser op, var der normalt ingen grund til, at aberne og Junglens Folk mødtes. Men når aberne fandt en syg ulv eller en såret tiger eller bjørn, plagede de ham. De kastede pinde og nødder efter alle dyr for sjov og i håb om, at nogen ville bemærke dem. De hylede og skreg meningsløse sange, de opfordrede Junglens Folk til at klatre op i deres træer og kæmpe, eller de gik i vilde slagsmål indbyrdes over ingenting og lod de døde ligge, hvor Junglens Folk kunne se dem. De var altid lige ved at vælge en leder og lave egne love og skikke. Det blev aldrig til noget, for de kunne ikke huske deres planer fra den ene dag til den næste. I stedet nøjedes de med et ordsprog, de selv havde fundet på: »Det, Bandar-log tænker i dag, tænker junglen i morgen.« Det trøstede dem meget. Ingen andre dyr kunne nå dem, men ingen andre dyr ville heller bemærke dem. Derfor var de blevet så glade for at lege med Mowgli, og derfor var de så glade for at høre, hvor vred Baloo var.

2.43.oldText: Det næste, han vidste, var, at små hænder — hårde, stærke hænder — greb fat om hans arme og ben. Grene strejfede hans ansigt. Så kiggede han ned gennem svajende grene, mens Baloos dybe råb vækkede junglen, og Bagheera for op ad træstammen med alle tænderne blottet. Bandar-log hylede triumferende og klatrede højere op på grene, hvor Bagheera ikke turde følge efter. »Han har lagt mærke til os!« råbte de. »Bagheera har lagt mærke til os. Hele Junglens Folk beundrer vores kløgt og dygtighed.« Så flygtede de. Ingen kan rigtig beskrive, hvordan Abefolket bevæger sig gennem træernes verden. De har deres egne veje og kryds over bakker og dale, alle sammen halvtreds, halvfjerds eller hundrede fod over jorden. De kan følge dem, selv når det er mørkt, hvis det er nødvendigt. To særligt stærke aber greb Mowgli under armene og svingede af sted med ham gennem trætoppene, hvor de tilbagelagde tyve fod i hvert spring. Uden ham kunne de have bevæget sig dobbelt så hurtigt, men hans vægt trak dem ned. Mowgli var svimmel og kvalm, men kunne alligevel ikke lade være med at nyde den vilde fart. Glimtene af jorden langt nede skræmte ham dog, og hvert forfærdeligt ryk, når en svingtur over tom luft blev standset, fik hans hjerte op i halsen. Aberne løb op ad et træ med ham, til han kunne mærke de tynde grene øverst knage og bøje sig under dem. Så kastede de sig med et host og et hvin ud og ned og greb fat i de nederste grene på det næste træ med hænder eller fødder. Nogle gange kunne han se milevidt ud over den stille grønne jungle, ligesom en mand i masten på et skib kan se milevidt ud over havet. Så pískede blade og grene ham i ansigtet, og han og hans to vogtere styrtede næsten ned til jorden igen. Hele Bandar-log-stammen fejede af sted ad vejene i træerne, med Mowgli som fange, og de sprang, brasede, hvinede og råbte.

2.44.oldText: I begyndelsen var han bange for, at de ville tabe ham. Så blev han vred, men havde forstand nok til ikke at kæmpe imod. Til sidst begyndte han at tænke. Han måtte få sendt besked til Baloo og Bagheera, for med den fart ville aberne snart efterlade hans venner langt bagude. Det nyttede ikke at kigge ned, for grenene skjulte alt undtagen deres overside. I stedet kiggede han op. Langt væk på den blå himmel svævede og kredsede glenten Rann og holdt øje med junglen, mens den ventede på, at noget skulle dø. Rann så, at aberne bar på en byrde, og dykkede nogle hundrede meter ned for at se, om det var noget at spise. Han fløjtede forbløffet, da Mowgli blev slæbt op i en trætop, og hørte ham råbe på Glentens sprog: »Vi er af ét blod, du og jeg.« De svajende grene slugte drengen igen, men Rann svævede over til det næste træ og nåede at se det lille brune ansigt dukke op igen. »Følg mit spor!« råbte Mowgli. »Sig til Baloo fra Seeonee-flokken og til Bagheera fra Rådsklippen.«

2.48.oldText: »De kommer aldrig særlig langt,« grinede han. »De gør aldrig færdigt, hvad de begynder på. Bandar-log hakker altid i noget nyt. Hvis mine øjne ikke svigter, har de denne gang hakket sig ud i vanskeligheder. Baloo er ingen kylling, og Bagheera kan, det ved jeg, dræbe større ting end geder.«

2.54.oldText: »Arrula! Whuu! Måske har de allerede tabt ham, trætte af hans vægt. Hvem kan stole på Bandar-log? Læg døde flagermus på mit hoved! Giv mig sorte knogler at spise! Rul mig ind i vilde biers reder, så de kan stikke mig ihjel, og begrav mig ved siden af Hyænen, for ingen bjørn har nogensinde været mere elendig end jeg! Arulala! Wahooa! Åh, Mowgli, Mowgli! Hvorfor bankede jeg dit hoved i stedet for at advare dig mod Abefolket? Måske har jeg slået dagens lektie helt ud af hans hoved. Måske er han nu helt alene i junglen og kan ikke huske Mesterordene.«

2.55.oldText: Baloo pressede poterne mod ørerne, vuggede fra side til side og stønnede.

2.56.oldText: »Han sagde i hvert fald alle Ordene rigtigt for mig for lidt siden,« sagde Bagheera utålmodigt. »Baloo, du har hverken hukommelse eller værdighed. Hvad ville junglen sige, hvis jeg, den sorte panter, rullede mig sammen som pindsvinet Ikki og begyndte at hyle?«

2.59.oldText: »Sikke en tåbe jeg er! Åh, sikke en fed, brun tåbe, der roder efter rødder,« råbte Baloo og rullede sig pludselig ud. »Den vilde elefant Hathi har ret, når han siger: ›Enhver har sin egen frygt.‹ Bandar-log er bange for Kaa, klippeslangen. Han kan klatre lige så godt som de, og om natten tager han de unge aber. Hvisk bare hans navn, så bliver deres slemme haler kolde. Vi må finde Kaa.«

2.63.oldText: »Hvis det kommer til stykket, gamle jæger, kan du og jeg sammen måske få ham til at høre på fornuft.« Baloo gned sin falmede brune skulder mod Panteren, og de to gik af sted for at finde Kaa, klippepytonen.

2.66.oldText: Kaa havde ikke gift. Han så faktisk ned på giftslanger som kujoner. Hans styrke lå i hans knugende favntag. Når først de vældige slyng lå om en, var der ikke mere at diskutere. »God jagt!« råbte Baloo og satte sig op på bagbenene. Ligesom andre af hans slags var Kaa lidt døv og hørte ikke den første hilsen. Så snoede han sig sammen, sænkede hovedet og gjorde sig klar til hvad som helst.

2.71.oldText: »Jeg er ret lang — ret lang,« sagde Kaa med et strejf af stolthed. »Alligevel er det dette nyvoksede træs skyld. På min sidste jagt var jeg ved at falde — meget nær, faktisk. Min hale var ikke viklet stramt nok om træet, og da jeg gled, vækkede larmen Bandar-log. De kaldte mig nogle virkelig grimme navne.«

2.72.oldText: »Fodløs, gul jordorm,« sagde Bagheera under sine knurhår, som om han forsøgte at huske noget.

2.77.oldText: »Det — det er dem, vi følger,« sagde Baloo. Det var næsten ved at kvæle ham at indrømme det. Så langt tilbage, han kunne huske, havde ingen af Junglens Folk nogensinde indrømmet at interessere sig for abernes gøren og laden.

2.79.oldText: »Ja,« begyndte Baloo, »jeg er bare den gamle og somme tider meget tåbelige Lovens Lærer for ulveungerne i Seeonee. Og hvad Bagheera her angår —«

2.81.oldText: »Ikki fortalte mig noget — de pigge gør ham alt for dristig — om et menneskevæsen, der var blevet optaget i en ulveflok. Jeg troede ikke på ham. Ikki gentager altid historier, han kun har hørt halvt, og han fortæller dem rigtig dårligt.«

2.86.oldText: »Orm — orm — jordorm,« rettede Bagheera ham. »Og andre ting, som jeg skammer mig for meget til at gentage.«

2.87.oldText: »Vi må minde dem om at tale pænt om deres herre. Aaa-ssp! Vi må hjælpe deres flakkende hukommelse. Nå, hvor gik de hen med ungen?«

2.88.oldText: »Det ved kun junglen. Mod solnedgang, tror jeg,« sagde Baloo. »Vi havde tænkt, at du måske vidste det, Kaa.«

2.89.oldText: »Jeg? Hvordan? Jeg tager dem, når de kommer i min vej, men jeg jager ikke Bandar-log — eller frøer — eller grønt skum på en vandpyt for den sags skyld.«

2.90.oldText: »Op, op! Op, op! Hillo! Illo! Illo, se herop, Baloo af Seeonee-ulveflokken!«

2.91.oldText: Baloo løftede blikket mod stemmen. Glenten Rann svævede ned, og solen fangede kanterne af hans vinger. Det var næsten hans sengetid, men han havde søgt over hele junglen efter Bjørnen uden at få øje på ham under det tætte løv.

2.93.oldText: »Jeg har set Mowgli blandt Bandar-log. Han bad mig fortælle jer det. Jeg holdt udkig. Bandar-log har taget ham over floden til abebyen — til De Kolde Huler. De bliver der måske én nat, eller ti nætter, eller en time. Jeg har bedt flagermusene holde vagt i mørketiden. Det er mit budskab. God jagt, alle I dernede!«

2.102.oldText: »Fødder eller ej, jeg kan følge med alle fire af jeres,« sagde Kaa skarpt. Baloo prøvede at sætte farten op, men måtte snart sætte sig ned og snappe efter vejret. De lod ham komme efter senere, og Bagheera ilede af sted i en panters rappe galop. Kaa sagde ingenting. Uanset hvor hårdt Bagheera anstrengte sig, holdt den enorme klippepyton trit med ham. Ved bjergbækkene kom Bagheera foran, for han sprang over, mens Kaa svømmede med hovedet og to fod af halsen over vandet. Men på flad jord indhentede Kaa ham igen.

2.103.oldText: »Ved den brudte lås, som satte mig fri,« udbrød Bagheera, da skumringen faldt på, »du ved sandelig, hvordan man kommer af sted!«

2.105.oldText: »Orm — jordorm, og oven i købet gul.«

2.111.oldText: Tyve eller tredive aber sprang af sted for at hente nødder og vilde papaja. Men undervejs begyndte de at slås, og det var for besværligt at bære den frugt, der var tilbage, med tilbage. Mowgli var øm, vred og sulten. Han vandrede gennem den forladte by og råbte fra tid til anden Fremmedes Jagtråb, men der kom intet svar. Han begyndte at føle, at han var havnet et rigtig forfærdeligt sted. »Baloo havde ret i alt,« tænkte han. »Bandar-log har ingen Lov, intet Jagtråb og ingen ledere — kun fjollet snak og små hænder, der snupper og stjæler. Hvis jeg sulter ihjel her, har jeg kun mig selv at bebrejde. På en eller anden måde må jeg tilbage til min egen jungle. Baloo vil sikkert tæve mig, men selv det er bedre end at løbe efter fjollede rosenblade sammen med Bandar-log.«

2.112.oldText: Så snart han nåede byens mur, slæbte aberne ham tilbage. De sagde, at han ikke satte pris på sin lykke, og knibede ham for at få ham til at føle sig taknemmelig. Han bed tænderne sammen uden et ord og fulgte den råbende skare op på en terrasse med udsigt over røde sandstensbassiner, der stadig var halvfulde af regnvand. I midten af terrassen stod en ødelagt sommerpavillon af hvidt marmor, bygget til dronninger, som havde været døde i hundrede år. Halvdelen af kuplen var styrtet sammen og havde blokeret den underjordiske gang fra paladset, som dronningerne engang var kommet ad. Men murene var skærme af udskåret marmor — smukt mælkehvidt gitterværk besat med agat, karneol, jaspis og lapis lazuli. Da månen kom op bag bakken, trængte lyset gennem åbningerne og tegnede skygger på jorden som broderi i sort fløjl. Så træt, sulten og øm han var, kunne Mowgli ikke lade være med at le, da tyve Bandar-log på én gang begyndte at forklare, hvor store, kloge, stærke og blide de var, og hvor tåbeligt det var af ham at ville forlade dem. »Vi er store. Vi er frie. Vi er vidunderlige. Intet folk i junglen er mere vidunderligt end os! Vi er alle enige, så det må være sandt,« råbte de. »Du er en ny tilhører, og du kan gentage vores ord for Junglens Folk, så de fra nu af vil lægge mærke til os. Derfor vil vi fortælle dig alt om vores fortræffelige selv.« Mowgli protesterede ikke. Hundredvis og atter hundredvis af aber trængtes på terrassen for at høre deres talere rose Bandar-log. Hver gang en taler løb tør for luft, råbte hele skaren: »Det er sandt; vi er alle enige.« Mowgli nikkede og blinkede og svarede »Ja«, hver gang de spurgte ham om noget, mens hans hoved snurrede af larmen. »Tabaqui Sjakalen må have bidt hver eneste af dem,« tænkte han, »og nu er de blevet gale. Det her må være _dewanee_, galskaben. Sover de aldrig? Nu trækker en sky ind foran månen. Hvis den bare var stor nok, kunne jeg prøve at flygte i mørket. Men jeg er så træt.«

2.114.oldText: »Jeg går til vestmuren,« hviskede Kaa, »og kommer hurtigt ned med jordens hældning til min fordel. De vil ikke kaste sig over min ryg i hundredvis, men —«

2.118.oldText: »Vi er af ét blod, du og jeg,« sagde Mowgli straks med Slangens Kald. Der lød raslen og hvæsen fra murbrokkerne rundt omkring. For at være sikker gentog han Kaldet.

2.119.oldText: »Jaaa, naturligvis! Sænk hætterne, alle sammen!« mumlede et halvt dusin stemmer. Før eller siden bliver enhver indisk ruin et hjem for slanger, og den gamle sommerpavillon vrimlede med kobraer. »Stå stille, Lillebror. Dine fødder kan gøre os fortræd.«

2.120.oldText: Mowgli stod så stille, han kunne, kiggede gennem de udskårne åbninger og lyttede til kampen, der rasede omkring den sorte panter. Skrig, pladren og slagsmål blandede sig med Bagheeras dybe, hæse host, mens han bakkede, bokkede, vred sig og kastede sig frem under bunker af fjender. Aldrig før i sit liv havde Bagheera måttet kæmpe blot for at holde sig i live.

2.122.oldText: Da Bagheera hørte Mowglis stemme og vidste, at drengen var i sikkerhed, fik han nyt mod. Fortvivlet kæmpede han sig tomme for tomme hen mod bassinerne og standsede fra tid til anden uden en lyd. Så lød Baloos rumlende krigsråb fra den ødelagte mur nærmest junglen. Den gamle Bjørn havde gjort alt, hvad han kunne, men var ikke nået frem før. »Bagheera,« råbte han, »nu kommer jeg! Jeg klatrer! Jeg skynder mig! Ahuwora! Stenene glider under mine poter! Bare vent, til jeg når dig, I skammelige Bandar-log!« Han kom stønnende og gispende op på terrassen og forsvandt op til hovedet under en bølge af aber. Han satte sig solidt på bagdelen, bredte forpoterne ud, tog så mange aber i favnen, som han kunne holde, og slog til i en jævn rytme, bat-bat-bat, som skovlene på et padlehjul. Mowgli hørte et brag og et plask: Bagheera var nået til bassinet, uden for abernes rækkevidde. Panteren lå og gispede med hovedet lige over vandet. På de røde trin stod aberne tre rækker dybt og hoppede op og ned af raseri, klar til at angribe ham fra alle sider, hvis han kom op for at hjælpe Baloo. Så løftede Bagheera sin dryppende hage og gav i fortvivlelse Slangens Kald om beskyttelse: »Vi er af ét blod, du og jeg.« Han troede, at Kaa var stukket af i sidste øjeblik. Selv Baloo, der næsten blev kvalt under aberne ved terrassens kant, kunne ikke lade være med at klukke, da han hørte den sorte panter bede om hjælp.

2.123.oldText: Kaa var netop kommet over vestmuren. Da han landede, sendte et ryk med kroppen en sten fra murkronen af sted ned i grøften. Han ville bevare enhver fordel, som terrænet gav, så han snoede sig sammen og ud igen et par gange for at tjekke, at hver eneste fod af hans lange krop virkede ordentligt. Hele den tid kæmpede Baloo stadig, aberne skreg omkring Bagheera i bassinet, og flagermusen Mang fløj frem og tilbage og bredte nyheden om det store slag ud over junglen. Selv elefanten Hathi trompeterede. Langt væk vågnede spredte flokke af Abefolket og kom springende ad træernes veje for at hjælpe deres venner i De Kolde Huler. Larmen vækkede alle dagfugle milevidt. Så stødte Kaa lige frem, hurtig og ivrig efter at dræbe. En python kæmper ved at slå med hovedet og lægge hele kroppens kraft og vægt bag slaget. Forestil dig en lanse, en rambuk eller en hammer, der vejer næsten et halvt ton, styret af et roligt, uhastet sind inde i skaftet. Så har du en idé om Kaa i kamp. Selv en python på fire eller fem fod kan vælte en mand med et direkte slag mod brystet, og Kaa var, som du ved, tredive fod lang. Hans første slag ramte midt ind i skaren omkring Baloo. Med lukket mund og helt tavs drev han det hjem. Der var ikke brug for et slag mere. Aberne spredtes og skreg: »Kaa! Det er Kaa! Løb! Løb!«

2.124.oldText: I generationer havde de ældre aber skræmt de unge til at opføre sig ordentligt med historier om Kaa, nattens tyv. De fortalte, hvordan han bevægede sig langs grenene lige så lydløst, som mos vokser, og tog den stærkeste abe, der fandtes. De fortalte om gamle Kaa, der kunne forklæde sig som en død gren eller en rådden stub, så selv de klogeste blev narret, indtil grenen greb dem. Han var alt det, aberne frygtede i junglen. Ingen af dem vidste, hvor langt hans magt rakte, ingen kunne møde hans blik, og ingen havde nogensinde overlevet hans favntag. Så de flygtede op på murene og hustagene og stammede af rædsel. Baloo pustede lettet ud. Hans pels var meget tykkere end Bagheeras, men kampen havde alligevel været hård ved ham. For første gang åbnede Kaa munden og udstødte ét langt, hvæsende ord. Langt væk stivnede de aber, der løb for at forsvare De Kolde Huler, hvor de var, og krøb sammen, indtil de overfyldte grene bøjede sig og knagede under deres vægt. De aber, der var på murene og i de tagløse huse, blev også stille. I stilheden over byen hørte Mowgli Bagheera ryste vandet af siderne, da han kom op af bassinet. Så begyndte larmen igen. Aberne klatrede højere op ad murene, klyngede sig til halsen på enorme stenafguder og skreg, mens de sprang langs murtinderne. Inde i sommerpavillonen dansede Mowgli, pressede øjet mod marmoråbningerne og huede som en ugle mellem fortænderne for at håne dem og vise sin foragt.

2.128.oldText: »Jeg er ikke sikker på, at de ikke har revet mig i hundrede små bjørne,« sagde Baloo højtideligt og rystede det ene ben efter det andet. »Av! Alt gør ondt. Kaa, jeg tror, du har reddet livet på os begge to — mit og Bagheeras.«

2.136.oldText: »Andre også,« sagde Bagheera og slikkede sig om munden og kiggede på de døde aber på terrassen og rundt om tanken.

2.139.oldText: Mowgli vendte sig om og så den store pythons hoved svaje en fod højere end hans eget.
